title: Pericardial Disease
subject: Cardiovascular System (CARD)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers the diseases of the sac around the heart: acute and secondary pericarditis, constrictive pericarditis, pericardial effusion, cardiac tamponade, and metastatic tumor in the pericardium. Each one is easiest to understand as a problem of diastolic filling inside a stiff bag, or as inflammation spreading to the epicardium beneath it. Board questions give a chest pain history, an ECG, a neck vein or blood pressure finding, or a clinical setting such as a recent infarct, renal failure, or known cancer, and ask you to name the process and explain the finding. If you understand the pericardial pressure-volume curve and ventricular interdependence, most of these questions answer themselves.
prerequisites: Layers of the pericardium and the mediastinum (CV-2, CV-3)

ECG leads, the ST segment, and the current of injury (CV-7)

connections.how: Transmural infarction causes early fibrinous pericarditis, Dressler syndrome weeks later, and hemopericardium when the free wall ruptures.
Restrictive cardiomyopathy produces the same filling limit as constrictive pericarditis from a stiff myocardium instead of a stiff sac, and viral myocarditis often accompanies viral pericarditis.
Uremia causes fibrinous pericarditis, and nephrotic syndrome causes transudative effusion through low oncotic pressure.
Coxsackie B, tuberculosis, pyogenic bacteria, lupus, and rheumatoid arthritis each injure the pericardium through a different mechanism and leave a different exudate.
Metastases to the heart greatly outnumber primary tumors such as myxoma and usually present through the pericardium.

Autoimmune pericarditis appearing weeks after myocardial infarction, thought to follow sensitization to released cardiac antigens.
Chronic fibrous, often calcified, thickening of the pericardium that encases the heart and limits diastolic filling.

An early diastolic sound produced when rapid ventricular filling stops abruptly against a rigid pericardium.

An inspiratory fall in systolic arterial pressure of more than 10 mmHg.
Beat-to-beat alternation of QRS amplitude or axis caused by the heart swinging within a large effusion.
The filling of one ventricle reducing the filling of the other because both share the septum and a fixed pericardial space.

blocks.text: The pericardium has an outer fibrous sac of dense collagen and an inner serous sac. The parietal serous layer lines the fibrous sac, and the visceral layer (the epicardium) covers the heart. Between them lies about 15 to 50 mL of serous fluid, a plasma ultrafiltrate that lets the heart move with little friction. The fibrous and parietal layers receive sensory fibers from the phrenic nerves (C3 to C5); the visceral layer is insensitive to pain.

Acute pericarditis is inflammation of these layers. In developed countries most cases are labeled idiopathic, and most idiopathic cases are presumed viral, because they follow a respiratory or gastrointestinal illness and behave like proven viral cases. Coxsackie B virus is the classic cause; echovirus, adenovirus, influenza, and HIV are others. Young and middle-aged adults, more often men, are typical. The virus and the host response raise vascular permeability, so fibrinogen escapes and polymerizes on both serous surfaces, giving a fibrinous or serofibrinous exudate that usually resolves without scarring.

Each classic finding follows from this inflammation. The pain is sharp and pleuritic because the inflamed parietal layer is stretched and rubbed with each heartbeat and breath; it worsens lying flat and with deep inspiration and eases on sitting up and leaning forward, which is thought to reduce pressure on the inflamed parietal surface. Phrenic innervation refers it to the trapezius ridge, a feature that ischemic pain lacks. Fibrin-coated layers grating together make the friction rub, a scratchy sound with up to three components (atrial systole, ventricular systole, and early diastolic filling), best heard at the lower left sternal border with the patient leaning forward. It comes and goes and can persist even when some fluid separates the layers. Low-grade fever, leukocytosis, and raised C-reactive protein reflect systemic inflammation; a troponin rise means the adjacent myocardium is inflamed (myopericarditis).

The pericardium itself generates no electrical signal. ECG changes come from inflammation of the superficial myocardium beneath the visceral layer. Injured epicardial cells create a current of injury that elevates the ST segment in leads facing the epicardium, and because the whole surface is involved, elevation appears in most limb and precordial leads rather than one coronary territory. Atrial epicardial injury displaces the PR segment, giving PR depression in most leads. Lead aVR looks into the cavities from above, so it shows the mirror image: ST depression and PR elevation. The changes evolve over days to weeks: diffuse ST elevation, then return of ST to baseline with T flattening, then T inversion, then normalization.

blocks.title: ECG of acute pericarditis versus ST elevation myocardial infarction
rows: Often while ST is still elevated
blocks.caption: Epicardial injury that covers the whole heart has no opposite wall to show reciprocal change, apart from leads that look into the cavity.

blocks.text: Most cases settle within weeks. The main complications are recurrence, effusion with tamponade (uncommon in idiopathic disease), and, rarely, later constriction.

blocks.predict: A 25-year-old with pleuritic chest pain has ST elevation in II, III, aVF, I, and V2 to V6, PR depression, and ST depression only in aVR. Why does this pattern argue against an inferior infarct?
blocks.explain: An inferior infarct elevates ST in II, III, and aVF and produces reciprocal depression in aVL and often I. Elevation in inferior, lateral, and anterior leads together with PR depression and no reciprocal change outside aVR indicates diffuse epicardial inflammation.

sections.title: Secondary pericarditis and the type of exudate

blocks.text: Secondary pericarditis arises from a disease outside the pericardium, and the exudate it produces reflects how strongly and in what way that disease injures the serosa. Mild injury with a modest rise in permeability yields serous fluid. Greater permeability lets fibrinogen escape, so fibrin coats the layers; the shaggy surface of severe fibrinous pericarditis is described as bread and butter. Organisms that recruit neutrophils produce pus. Damaged vessels, fragile tumor vessels, or a bleeding tendency add blood. Granulomatous infection produces caseous necrosis.

blocks.title: Causes of secondary pericarditis and their usual exudate
rows: Necrosis of a transmural infarct inflames the overlying pericardium
Fibrinous or fibrinohemorrhagic, over the infarct
Autoimmune reaction to released cardiac antigens
Direct trauma; later a Dressler-like post-pericardiotomy syndrome
Retained metabolic toxins injure the serosa
Fibrinous; hemorrhagic with uremic platelet dysfunction
Endothelial and serosal injury; later fibrosis
Spread from pneumonia or empyema, blood, or surgery
Tumor implants with fragile vessels and blocked lymphatics
blocks.caption: Fibrinous and serofibrinous exudates are the most common; purulent and caseous exudates are the most likely to organize into constriction.

blocks.text: The two forms after infarction differ in timing and mechanism. Early pericarditis appears within the first few days over a transmural infarct, because the necrosis reaches the epicardium; it is localized, fibrinous, and self-limited. It is not expected with subendocardial infarcts, which spare the epicardium. Dressler syndrome appears weeks later and is systemic: fever, pleuritis, and pericarditis with effusion. Its timing fits an adaptive immune response rather than direct injury, and the same picture after cardiac surgery is called post-pericardiotomy syndrome.

blocks.title: Dressler syndrome as an immune reaction to injury
steps: Infarction or surgery injures myocardium and pericardium
Hidden myocardial antigens are released
Antibodies and T cells are primed over weeks
Immune attack on pericardium and pleura
Fever, pleuritic pain, rub, and effusion weeks later
blocks.caption: The delay of weeks is what separates Dressler syndrome from early post-infarction pericarditis.

blocks.text: Uremic pericarditis develops in severe renal failure from retained toxins rather than infection. Because the inflammation tends not to involve the epicardial myocardium, the typical diffuse ST elevation is often absent, and uremic platelet dysfunction makes the fluid bloody and more likely to cause tamponade. Bacterial pericarditis, usually Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pneumoniae, reaches the pericardium by spread from a pneumonia or empyema, through the blood, or after chest surgery, and it is acute and toxic. Tuberculous pericarditis spreads from mediastinal lymph nodes and is chronic, caseous, and often hemorrhagic. These two, together with radiation, are the forms most likely to heal by dense fibrosis and constriction.

Constrictive pericarditis is the chronic end of pericardial inflammation. Granulation tissue organizes the exudate, the layers fuse and obliterate the space, and dense fibrous tissue, sometimes calcified, forms a rigid shell around the heart. Worldwide, tuberculosis is a major cause. In developed countries most cases follow idiopathic or viral pericarditis, cardiac surgery, or mediastinal radiation, for example for Hodgkin lymphoma.

blocks.title: From pericarditis to constriction
steps: Fibrinous, purulent, or caseous exudate
Granulation tissue organizes the exudate
Visceral and parietal layers fuse
Dense fibrosis, sometimes with calcification
Rigid shell fixes the total cardiac volume
blocks.caption: Organization of exudate replaces a compliant sac with a fixed shell.

blocks.text: The shell sets a fixed limit on total cardiac volume, but the myocardium inside relaxes normally. In early diastole the ventricles fill very rapidly, driven by high atrial pressure, until they reach the limit of the shell, where filling stops abruptly. The sudden halt makes the pericardial knock, an early diastolic sound that comes earlier and is higher pitched than an S3. On ventricular pressure tracings the same event appears as a dip-and-plateau (square root) pattern, and the jugular venous pulse shows a steep y descent. Diastolic pressures in all four chambers rise and become nearly equal. Systolic function is preserved, but the limited filling lowers stroke volume, and the high venous pressure produces hepatomegaly, ascites, and edema out of proportion to lung congestion. Plain films or CT may show pericardial calcification.

Kussmaul sign is the jugular venous pressure rising, or failing to fall, during inspiration. Normally inspiration lowers intrathoracic pressure, the fall is transmitted to the right atrium, and venous return is drawn in, so the neck veins fall. In constriction the rigid shell blocks transmission of intrathoracic pressure to the heart, while descent of the diaphragm still pushes more abdominal venous blood toward a right heart that cannot expand, so venous pressure rises. The same isolation causes reciprocal filling: the pulmonary veins lie outside the shell, so inspiration lowers their pressure but not left heart pressure, and left filling falls while the extra right ventricular volume pushes the septum left. Kussmaul sign is not specific; it also occurs in restrictive cardiomyopathy and right ventricular infarction.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy produces a very similar filling limit, but the stiffness lies in a myocardium infiltrated or scarred by amyloid, sarcoidosis, hemochromatosis, or endomyocardial fibrosis, and the pericardium is normal.

blocks.title: Constrictive pericarditis versus restrictive cardiomyopathy
rows: Normal or mildly raised (shell limits myocardial stretch)
Low voltage with conduction disease suggests amyloid
blocks.caption: Both limit filling with preserved ejection fraction and show dip-and-plateau tracings; the location of the stiffness explains every difference.

blocks.predict: Why do the two ventricles fill reciprocally with breathing in constriction but not in restrictive cardiomyopathy?
blocks.explain: In constriction total cardiac volume is fixed by the shell, so more right ventricular filling on inspiration pushes the septum left and reduces left ventricular filling. The pulmonary veins lie outside the shell and their pressure falls with inspiration, which further lowers left heart filling. In restrictive cardiomyopathy the pericardium is compliant and each stiff ventricle limits only its own filling.

sections.title: Pericardial effusion: causes, findings, and the rate of accumulation

blocks.text: A pericardial effusion is fluid in excess of the normal 15 to 50 mL. Its composition points to the cause. Serous effusions are transudates that form when Starling forces shift: raised venous pressure in heart failure, or low plasma oncotic pressure in nephrotic syndrome and cirrhosis. Hypothyroidism produces a large, slowly forming, protein-rich effusion through increased capillary leak and reduced lymphatic drainage. Exudates come from the pericarditis causes in C02. Hemorrhagic fluid points to trauma, free wall rupture, aortic dissection, malignancy, tuberculosis, uremia, or a bleeding tendency.

The fibrous pericardium has a J-shaped pressure-volume curve. Over the small reserve volume, added fluid barely raises pressure; beyond it, collagen fibers straighten and pressure climbs steeply. Fluid added over minutes reaches the steep limb at once, so as little as about 150 to 200 mL can compress the heart. Fluid that collects over weeks to months lets the sac stretch and remodel, shifting the curve to the right, so a liter or more can accumulate with little rise in pressure. For this reason the speed of accumulation predicts compression better than the volume.

blocks.title: Why rate matters more than volume
blocks.text: Patient A has hypothyroidism and 1,200 mL of pericardial fluid that built up over four months; her blood pressure is normal. Patient B has a stab wound and 200 mL of blood that collected in 20 minutes; he is hypotensive with distended neck veins. In A, slow stretch enlarged the sac, so pericardial pressure stayed below right atrial pressure (about 2 to 6 mmHg) and filling continued. In B, the sac had no time to stretch, so 200 mL pushed pericardial pressure up the steep limb past right atrial and right ventricular diastolic pressure. The chamber with the lowest pressure stops filling first, and output falls. Volume alone would have predicted the opposite outcome.

blocks.title: Findings of a large effusion and their mechanism
rows: Fluid separates the heart from the chest wall and dampens sound
Fluid separates the inflamed layers, though a rub can persist
Low-voltage QRS (all limb leads under 5 mm)
Fluid between heart and electrodes attenuates the signal
The heart swings within a large effusion, changing its axis on alternate beats
Fluid fills the sac; usually needs more than about 250 mL to show
Fluid separates the visceral and parietal layers
blocks.caption: Low voltage is not specific (obesity, emphysema, hypothyroidism, amyloid); electrical alternans in this setting suggests a large effusion and possible tamponade.

blocks.text: A large chronic effusion can be well tolerated while still producing these signs, and lung fields are usually clear because left heart pressures are not raised. The signs describe the amount of fluid; whether filling is impaired depends on pericardial pressure, which is the subject of tamponade.

Tamponade is a hemodynamic state, not a fluid volume: it exists once pericardial pressure rises enough to impair filling. Any effusion can cause it, but the classic acute cause is hemopericardium. Penetrating trauma often enters the right ventricle, the most anterior chamber. Free wall rupture after transmural infarction, most often about 3 to 7 days after the event when macrophages have softened the necrotic wall, causes sudden tamponade and pulseless electrical activity. Type A aortic dissection can rupture backward into the sac, because the proximal ascending aorta lies inside the pericardial reflection. Nontraumatic causes also include malignancy, uremia, and pericarditis.

blocks.title: How rising pericardial pressure lowers cardiac output
steps: Fluid or blood collects faster than the sac can stretch
Pericardial pressure exceeds right heart diastolic pressure
Right atrium and ventricle collapse in diastole
Diastolic pressures in all chambers equalize with pericardial pressure
Preload and stroke volume fall; tachycardia compensates
Hypotension, distended neck veins, distant heart sounds
blocks.caption: The thin-walled, low-pressure right heart is compressed first.

blocks.text: All four chambers sit inside one tense sac, so their diastolic pressures (right atrial, right ventricular diastolic, pulmonary artery diastolic, and pulmonary capillary wedge) become nearly equal to pericardial pressure. Filling now occurs mainly during ventricular systole, when ejection briefly lowers intrapericardial volume and pressure; the jugular x descent is preserved and the y descent is blunted or absent. Beck triad follows: hypotension from low stroke volume, distended neck veins from high venous pressure, and distant heart sounds from the fluid. Sinus tachycardia is the compensating response, and electrical alternans may appear.

blocks.title: Pulsus paradoxus in tamponade
steps: Inspiration lowers intrathoracic pressure
Venous return to the right ventricle increases
Right ventricle cannot expand outward against the tense sac
Septum bulges into the left ventricle
Pulmonary veins also hold more blood on inspiration
Left ventricular filling and stroke volume fall
Systolic pressure drops more than 10 mmHg
blocks.caption: Total cardiac volume is fixed, so right heart gain on inspiration becomes left heart loss.

blocks.text: Pulsus paradoxus is an exaggeration of the normal small inspiratory fall in systolic pressure, made large by ventricular interdependence. It is not specific to tamponade: severe asthma, COPD, and massive pulmonary embolism produce it through large swings in intrathoracic pressure or right ventricular strain. Kussmaul sign is usually absent in tamponade, because the fluid still transmits the inspiratory fall in intrathoracic pressure to the right atrium.

blocks.title: Measuring pulsus paradoxus
blocks.text: The cuff is inflated above systolic pressure and deflated slowly while the patient breathes quietly. At 122 mmHg the first Korotkoff sounds appear only during expiration. Deflation continues until, at 98 mmHg, sounds are heard with every beat in both phases of breathing. The pulsus is 122 minus 98, or 24 mmHg, more than 10 mmHg and therefore abnormal. The beats lost on inspiration are those with the smallest left ventricular stroke volume, which is the interdependence described above. With jugular venous distension and muffled heart sounds, this points to tamponade.

blocks.title: Tamponade versus constrictive pericarditis
blocks.caption: Fluid compresses the heart throughout diastole; a shell stops filling only once its limit is reached.

blocks.predict: A patient 5 days after a large anterior infarct suddenly becomes hypotensive with distended neck veins and an organized rhythm on the monitor but no pulse. What happened and why is there no pulse?
blocks.explain: Free wall rupture has filled the pericardium with blood. Pericardial pressure exceeds diastolic pressure in every chamber, so the ventricles cannot fill and stroke volume approaches zero even though electrical activity continues (pulseless electrical activity).

sections.title: Metastatic disease of the heart and pericardium

blocks.text: Tumors that reach the heart from elsewhere are far more common than primary cardiac tumors such as myxoma; autopsy series find cardiac or pericardial metastases in roughly 5 to 10% of patients who die of cancer. The pericardium is the most frequent site, followed by the epicardium and myocardium. Because lung and breast carcinoma are common and lie next to the heart, they account for the largest numbers of cases. Melanoma, by contrast, is less common but involves the heart in a high proportion of patients with widespread disease, and leukemia and lymphoma often infiltrate it.

blocks.title: Routes of spread to the heart
rows: Lung carcinoma, breast carcinoma, esophageal carcinoma, mediastinal tumors
Retrograde lymphatic spread through mediastinal nodes
Growth along the inferior vena cava into the right atrium
blocks.caption: Proximity explains lung and breast; wide bloodstream spread explains melanoma and the hematologic cancers.

blocks.text: Pericardial deposits produce effusion through two mechanisms. Tumor implants on the serosa have fragile, leaky new vessels that bleed, and tumor blocking the mediastinal lymphatics prevents the normal drainage of pericardial fluid. The result is a hemorrhagic exudate that keeps accumulating, often to tamponade; malignancy is one of the most common causes of nontraumatic tamponade. Finding malignant cells on cytology of the pericardial fluid confirms the cause.

The clinical picture follows from the fluid. Patients usually present with progressive dyspnea, chest discomfort, and the effusion signs in C04, and a rapidly growing effusion or one that keeps reaccumulating after drainage raises suspicion of tumor.

blocks.title: From pericardial metastasis to tamponade
steps: Tumor reaches the pericardium by extension, lymphatics, or blood
Serosal implants with fragile new vessels bleed
Lymphatic obstruction blocks fluid drainage
Bloody exudate with malignant cells accumulates
Pericardial pressure rises until filling fails
blocks.caption: Effusion forms faster than it drains, so it tends to recur and progress.

blocks.text: Two related problems complete the picture. Tumor that encases the heart can behave like constrictive pericarditis, and mediastinal radiation given for the same cancer can later cause radiation pericarditis and constriction, so a pericardial problem in a patient with cancer is not always due to tumor. Myocardial deposits are less often symptomatic but can disturb conduction and cause arrhythmias, and intracavitary tumor can obstruct flow.

integration.text: Across pericardial disease, anatomy and physiology explain the findings and pathology explains the causes. The fibrous pericardium is a stiff collagen bag with a J-shaped pressure-volume curve, so whether fluid compresses the heart depends on how fast it arrives, and a shared, fixed space makes the two ventricles compete for volume, which produces pulsus paradoxus and reciprocal respiratory filling. The pathology of the exudate links the pericardium to microbiology and immunology: viruses and immune complexes give serous or fibrinous fluid, pyogenic bacteria give pus, tuberculosis gives caseation, and tumors and bleeding give blood.

The limits of each sign matter. Diffuse ST elevation can be absent in uremic pericarditis, low voltage has many causes, Kussmaul sign occurs in restrictive cardiomyopathy and right ventricular infarction as well as constriction, and pulsus paradoxus occurs in severe asthma and pulmonary embolism. Constriction and restriction look alike at the bedside and are separated by where the stiffness lies, sac or muscle.

summary: Acute pericarditis is usually idiopathic or viral (coxsackie B) and gives pleuritic pain eased by leaning forward, a friction rub, diffuse concave ST elevation, and PR depression, with the mirror image in aVR.
The pericardium is electrically silent; ECG changes come from inflammation of the underlying epicardium, which is why they span coronary territories without reciprocal depression.

The exudate reflects the cause: fibrinous after infarction, in Dressler syndrome, and in uremia; serous or fibrinous in lupus; purulent with bacteria; caseous with tuberculosis; hemorrhagic with cancer.
Early post-infarction pericarditis appears within days over a transmural infarct; Dressler syndrome appears weeks later as an autoimmune reaction to released cardiac antigens.

Constrictive pericarditis is a rigid, often calcified shell that stops filling abruptly in early diastole, producing a pericardial knock, steep y descent, Kussmaul sign, and equal diastolic pressures.
Restrictive cardiomyopathy limits filling from a stiff myocardium with a normal pericardium, markedly raised natriuretic peptide, and little reciprocal respiratory variation.
Pericardial pressure depends on the rate of accumulation: about 150 to 200 mL added acutely can cause tamponade, while a liter or more collected slowly may not.
Tamponade lowers output by preventing filling; Beck triad, pulsus paradoxus over 10 mmHg, a blunted y descent, and equal diastolic pressures follow from compression inside a fixed sac.

Metastases to the heart greatly outnumber primary tumors; lung, breast, melanoma, lymphoma, and leukemia reach the pericardium and produce a bloody effusion with malignant cells that can cause tamponade.

verify: Normal pericardial fluid volume is quoted from about 15 to 50 mL across sources; confirm the range NABNE uses.
Volumes for acute tamponade (about 150 to 200 mL) and for radiographic enlargement (more than about 250 mL) are approximate and vary between sources.

Timing of early post-infarction pericarditis (about 1 to 3 days) and of Dressler syndrome (usually given as about 2 to 10 weeks) differs slightly between texts; Dressler syndrome has become uncommon since early reperfusion.
Timing of free wall rupture (most often about 3 to 7 days, range up to about 2 weeks) should match the figure used in CV-18-C.
The statement that uremic pericarditis often lacks diffuse ST elevation is standard clinical teaching but is not stated in every pathology text.
The autopsy frequency of cardiac metastases in patients dying of cancer (roughly 5 to 10%) and the ratio of metastatic to primary cardiac tumors vary widely between series.
The pain relief on leaning forward is traditionally attributed to reduced pressure on the inflamed parietal pericardium; the mechanism is not firmly established.
Low-voltage QRS criteria (under 5 mm in all limb leads, under 10 mm in all precordial leads) are the usual definition; confirm the values NABNE expects.
Confirm whether NABNE expects echocardiographic and natriuretic peptide criteria for separating constriction from restriction or only the bedside and pathologic distinctions.

Requested new diagram names for a future revision: pericardial-pv-curve (acute versus chronic pericardial pressure-volume curves) and jvp-tamponade-constriction (jugular venous waveforms showing a blunted y descent in tamponade and a steep y descent in constriction).
